title:
Works on
our machines.
subtitle: An introduction to Docker
notes: Ask: who has cloned a project that failed to run? Let two students describe the error. Today we will package a small app and its runtime, then run it with a separate data service. Plan: 90 minutes including discussion and lab. Cover artwork is a generated illustration, not a real class photograph.

title:
Same code.
Different environments.
left:
Python is installed.
Redis is running.
The settings are right.
right:
A different Python version.
No Redis service.
A missing environment variable.
bottom: The code travels. Its environment needs to travel too.
notes: Use an example: the source is identical, but Redis is missing. Ask what else the app needs besides code. Capture runtime, dependencies, configuration, OS/architecture, and external services. Packaging reduces environment drift; it does not eliminate every difference.

title:
A virtual machine
is a whole computer.
statement:
Virtual hardware.
A separate guest kernel.
rows: Virtual CPUs, RAM, disks and network interfaces use the physical host.
Allocates hardware resources to each guest.
Boots and runs its own kernel and user-space programs.
bottom: HOST = the real machine     /     GUEST = the virtual machine
notes: Explain host versus guest. Virtual hardware uses the real machine’s resources through a hypervisor. A guest OS must still be installed, booted, patched, and stored. Source: https://www.redhat.com/en/topics/virtualization/what-is-virtualization

title: Two kinds of hypervisor
left:
Runs at the hardware layer.

Examples: KVM, VMware ESXi.
right:
Runs through a host OS.

Examples: VirtualBox,
VMware Workstation.
bottom: Both provide virtual hardware. Their placement differs.
notes: Examples: KVM is integrated into Linux; VMware ESXi is a familiar bare-metal example. VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are hosted examples. Hardware virtualization support helps guests execute efficiently. Do not imply every instruction is interpreted in software. Source: https://www.redhat.com/en/topics/virtualization/what-is-virtualization

title: When a VM makes sense
rows: Run an Ubuntu lab on a Windows laptop.
Provision a server with a separate operating system.
Test a kernel or support a legacy environment.
bottom: Tradeoff: another OS to store, boot, allocate memory to and patch.
notes: Ask why a university might issue one VM per student. Separate guest kernels permit distinct OS environments. VM snapshots and isolated experiments can help teaching and administration. VMs are still software and can have vulnerabilities. Source: https://www.redhat.com/en/topics/virtualization/what-is-virtualization These are tradeoffs, not claims that VMs are bad or always slow. Actual overhead and startup times depend on the workload and platform. VMs can be the right isolation boundary when separate kernels are required. Source: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/

title:
A container
is an isolated process.
statement:
App + dependencies.
A shared Linux kernel.
rows: Separate views of processes, filesystems and networking.
Account for resources and enforce configured limits.
Supply the application and user-space files.
bottom: An Ubuntu image contains Ubuntu user space, not its own booted kernel.
notes: Examples: a Python API, Nginx web server, and Redis data service can each run in a container. The container image supplies user-space files, not a separate kernel. On a non-Linux laptop the Linux kernel is supplied by a Linux environment/VM. Source: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/ Namespaces isolate views; cgroups handle resource accounting and configured limits. Limits are not a promise that every container has a useful CPU/RAM cap by default. Isolation also depends on capabilities, permissions, and kernel security features. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/ ; https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-an-image/

title: A smaller unit to distribute
left:
Package runtime dependencies.
Reuse filesystem layers.
Start application processes.
right:
Kernel and CPU compatibility.
Configuration and services.
Permissions and resource limits.
bottom: Examples: a Python API, an Nginx web server, a Redis data service.
notes: Common uses: reproducible development setups, CI test environments, and distributing services. Containers often have lower per-app overhead than full VMs. Avoid universal speed or size numbers. Architecture, kernel compatibility, config and external services still affect behavior. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/ ; https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-an-image/ Security: https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/

title: The kernel is the key difference
body:
VMs keep guest kernels separate.
Containers share a kernel.
notes: Concept illustration generated for teaching, with labels checked against https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/ and https://www.redhat.com/en/topics/virtualization/what-is-virtualization. Linux containers are the scope here. Do not infer that containers inherently provide the same boundary as separate VMs.

title: Two useful isolation boundaries
bottom: Lower per-app overhead is common with containers; actual results depend on the workload.
notes: Read the kernel row first. Typical isolation differs; neither is an unconditional security guarantee. Linux images require a Linux kernel and compatible CPU architecture or emulation. Sources: https://www.redhat.com/en/topics/virtualization/what-is-virtualization ; https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/ ; https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/

title: Containers inside VMs
statement:
The VM hosts the machine.
Containers package its apps.
rows: One VM can run several containerized services.
On a Mac or Windows PC
Desktop supplies a Linux environment for these Linux containers.
Docker Engine can use the host’s Linux kernel directly.
bottom: Docker Desktop for Linux also uses its own VM and context.
notes: The VM provides a machine boundary; containers package applications within it. Docker Desktop for Linux also runs a VM, whereas native Linux Engine can run directly on the host kernel. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/ ; https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/linux/ ; https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/windows-install/ ; https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/mac-install/

title: Docker is the toolkit
rows: Turn a Dockerfile and build context into an image.
Pull and push images through a registry.
Create and manage containers from images.
bottom: Docker makes containers usable across development, testing and deployment.
notes: Docker is a platform around containers, not a synonym for all container technology. Explain that the docker command is a client talking to an engine. Compose will describe our two-service application. Source: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/

title: Five core Docker concepts
rows: The docker CLI sends requests to the engine.
dockerd manages containers, images, networks and volumes.
A runnable instance of an image.
Stores images; Docker Hub is one example.
bottom: A teaching grouping, not an exhaustive list. Compose connects the services in this lab.
notes: This is a teaching grouping of five concepts, not an exhaustive or officially fixed component count. docker is the CLI client; dockerd is the daemon. Docker Hub is one registry. Networks, volumes, Buildx and Compose also matter. Source: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/

title: A command reaches the engine
body:
CLIENT → DAEMON → IMAGE / CONTAINER
Pulls and pushes also involve a registry.
notes: Trace docker pull from client to daemon to registry, then docker run from a local image to a container. The registry stores images; it does not run the classroom containers. Image source and technical reference: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/ ; https://docs.docker.com/get-started/images/docker-architecture.webp . Docker illustration © Docker Inc., used with attribution for teaching.

title: An image tag is a label
rows: Image repository: Docker Hub’s official Redis image.
One tag: Redis 7.4 on an Alpine Linux base.
bottom: python:3.13-slim = Python 3.13 with a smaller Debian user-space base.
notes: Image syntax: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/tag/ ; image variants: https://hub.docker.com/_/python ; https://hub.docker.com/_/redis . Tags may change. Omitting a tag defaults to latest, which is not a promise of newest. Digests pin content. redis:6379 is a host:port address, not an image tag.

title: Your first Dockerfile
rows: Where should the app live inside the image?
Which file lists dependencies? Copy it first.
Install requirements with pip; explain -r and the cache.
Put app.py, templates and static together.
bottom: Create Dockerfile at the repository root. Finish USER, EXPOSE and CMD using the lab.
notes: Student exercise, not a finished file to run. Begin with app/app.py and requirements.txt. Main checkout intentionally lacks root Dockerfile, .dockerignore and compose.yaml. Students fill the scaffold in docs/lab.md and explain each instruction; complete reference is in solutions/Dockerfile after attempting. COPY requirements.txt . precedes RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt; COPY app/ . follows. WORKDIR /app, base python:3.13-slim. Next slide explains runtime flags for their CMD. Reference: https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/ .

title: Starting the web process
rows: Numeric user ID : group ID. Avoid a root web process.
Document the container port; does not publish it.
Listen on all container interfaces, port 8000.
Two workers; send access logs to stdout.
Python module : application object, not an image tag.
bottom: CMD in the Dockerfile uses a JSON argument list to launch this server at runtime.
notes: CMD is the default startup command. Each JSON string is an argument; no shell expansion occurs. --bind takes a listening address, --workers takes a count, --access-logfile takes a destination, and - means stdout here. 0.0.0.0 inside a container is distinct from the host loopback binding. Source: repository Dockerfile; https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/ .

title: Write the two-service Compose file
rows: Publish web only: host loopback → port 8000.
Use the other service name, not localhost.
Select Redis 7.4 on Alpine using its image tag.
Validate your YAML before starting anything.
bottom: Create compose.yaml in the root. Add persistence and health checks in later exercises.
notes: Students create compose.yaml from the scaffold in docs/lab.md. Keep exactly two services, web and redis. Minimal stage: build ., ports 127.0.0.1:8000:8000, REDIS_HOST redis, image redis:7.4-alpine. Initial startup may need a moment for Redis; health checks come later. Do not publish Redis. config validates/prints resolved YAML. Main checkout intentionally lacks an active Compose file; solutions/compose.yaml is an instructor answer key. Later tasks add counter-data:/data, AOF, healthchecks and depends_on service_healthy. Source: repository lab and https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/ .

title: Installation routes
left:
Windows, macOS or supported Linux.

Engine + CLI + Buildx + Compose
with a graphical dashboard.
right:
Install individual packages.

CLI + daemon + runtime + plugins.
Useful on workstations and servers.
bottom: A Docker CLI alone cannot run containers without access to an engine.
notes: Choose one route before class. Desktop is convenient for Windows/macOS. Native Engine is useful on Linux workstations and servers. A CLI alone cannot run containers without an accessible engine. Full prerequisites and commands: docs/installation.md. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/ ; https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/linux/

title: Desktop setup by operating system
rows:
Supported WSL 2, hardware virtualization, Linux containers.
Enable integration for the WSL distro you will use.

Download for Apple silicon or Intel.
Open the installer, install and launch Docker.

Supported distro + KVM.
Desktop runs a separate VM and image store.
bottom: Launch Desktop and wait for the engine. Current requirements: docs/installation.md.
notes: Verify the current supported OS versions and hardware requirements at the linked pages. Windows users working in WSL should enable integration for their distribution. macOS: open DMG, drag to Applications, launch. Linux: follow its distro-specific package guide; Desktop has a separate VM/context. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/windows-install/ ; https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/mac-install/ ; https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/linux/ wsl --version prints its version; wsl --status reports its configuration. Full OS-specific setup is linked in docs/installation.md.

title: Native Linux packages
code:
sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io \
  docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
bottom: Ubuntu: apt install. Fedora: dnf install. Configure the matching official repository first.
notes: The backslash continues the apt command onto the next shell line; this is one command. sudo runs as administrator; apt is Ubuntu’s package manager; install requests installation; following names are package arguments. Fedora uses sudo dnf install with the same names. Never use Ubuntu repository setup on Fedora. Backslash is a POSIX shell line continuation, not part of a package name. Full repository/key setup, systemctl enable --now docker and Linux group access are decoded in docs/installation.md. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/ ; https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/fedora/ .

title: Can this terminal use Docker?
rows: Client + Server: CLI can reach an engine.

run creates a container; --rm removes it on exit;
hello-world is the image (default tag latest).
List engine contexts; check which one is active.
bottom: Client only? Start the engine. Permission denied? Check native Linux access.
notes: An additional check is docker info, which displays the selected engine’s details. version displays versions; context manages connection configurations; ls lists contexts; info shows engine details. Native Engine users may need sudo. Also git --version prints Git’s version. hello-world checks pull/run, not the project build/network. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/ ; https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/ .

title: The command line has a grammar
rows: Docker CLI + the Compose plugin. Reads compose.yaml.
Create and start the configured services.
Detach: leave services running in the background.
Build custom service images before starting.
bottom: No service argument here → run the app’s services together.
notes: Run this only after students have written compose.yaml. Standard local workflow. Unlike attached up, detached up returns the terminal. --build does not force downloading every newer base image. Optional automated alternative --wait waits for running/healthy and implies detached mode. Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/up/

title: Container status
rows: List this project’s service containers and their status.
Include stopped containers as well as running ones.
Running means a process exists. Healthy means its probe passes.
bottom: Start with ps, then open http://localhost:8000 when both services are healthy.
notes: docker compose prefix: CLI plus plugin. No service filter here, so inspect the project’s containers. In the initial check, plain ps is enough for running services. -a helps diagnose the stopped Redis exercise. Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/ps/

title: Reading container logs
rows: Keep displaying new output as it arrives.
Start with the most recent 20 lines per container.
Service argument: show the web service only.
bottom: Ctrl+C exits this log viewer. Already-detached services continue running.
notes: 20 is a value for --tail, not a service name. Without -f this is a snapshot and exits. Without web, include all services. Compare Ctrl+C during attached docker compose up, which stops its attached app. Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/logs/

title: A command inside a container
code: docker compose exec redis redis-cli GET visits
rows: Run a process in an existing running service container.
Service argument: choose the Redis container.
Program to execute inside that container.
Redis command GET; key argument visits.
bottom: For a shell: docker compose exec web sh — web selects the service; sh is the program.
notes: The program’s arguments begin after the service name. Compose exec allocates an interactive terminal by default. In sh, pwd prints working directory, printenv REDIS_HOST prints that variable, exit leaves the shell without stopping Gunicorn. -T disables terminal allocation in scripts. Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/exec/

title: Build, pull, then run
rows: build creates the custom image; web selects the service.
pull downloads the configured image; redis selects it.
Create/recreate and start services using the images.
List images used by created service containers.
Validate and print the resolved app configuration.
bottom: build and pull prepare images. They do not replace a running service by themselves.
notes: docker compose = CLI + plugin throughout. -d = detach. A service argument selects a configured service, not an image repository. config --quiet validates without printing, useful in CI. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/build/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/pull/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/up/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/images/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/

title: Stop, start or restart?
rows: Halt the Redis container. Keep the container.
Start that existing stopped Redis container.
Stop then start the existing web container.
bottom:
restart does not rebuild an image or apply changed Compose configuration.
After a source edit: docker compose up -d --build.
notes: stop/start/restart are the actions; redis/web select services. start does not create a missing container. In up -d --build, -d detaches, --build builds configured images first, and up recreates the changed service. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/stop/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/start/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/restart/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/up/

title: A container is not its data
left:
Stops/removes the service containers
and project network.
Keeps our named volume.
right:
Same cleanup, plus removal of the
project’s declared named volume.
The saved count is deleted.
bottom: A volume is persistent storage. It is not a backup.
notes: docker compose = CLI + plugin; down is the cleanup action; --volumes (short -v here) adds volume removal. External volumes are not removed. No host-wide prune is needed. Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/down/

title: Three files you create
rows: Choose the base, paths, dependency install and startup command.
Choose which files enter the build context. Then build and run.
Build web, pull Redis and connect the services.
bottom: No active Docker configuration is supplied in the main checkout. Start in docs/lab.md.
notes: Students author three root files. Completed reference is isolated in solutions/ and CI materializes it only in its disposable checkout. First build: docker build -t classroom-web:workshop . ; build creates image, -t assigns repository:tag, final dot is context. First run: docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 classroom-web:workshop; --rm removes after exit, -p publishes IP:host-port:container-port. Standalone /health returns 503 because Redis is absent; a crash is not a passing checkpoint. Stop attached run with Ctrl+C before Compose uses port 8000. https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/buildx/build/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/

title: Improve the files you wrote
rows: Observe lost state, then add a named volume and Redis AOF.
Add health checks and wait for healthy Redis at startup.
Rebuild an edit. Stop Redis, inspect logs, then recover.
bottom: Predict the outcome, change one thing, run it, then explain the evidence.
notes: Use docs/lab.md. First minimal Compose has no named volume: down/up loses the old count. Add top-level counter-data volume, mount /data, and redis-server --appendonly yes --appendfsync always. Then configure Redis ping health, web urllib /health health, depends_on redis condition service_healthy. Rebuild after HTML edit using up -d --build; restart alone does not update the image. Stop/start redis demonstrates 503 and recovery. down removes containers/network but retains named data; --volumes explicitly deletes it. Compare solutions only after attempting each checkpoint.

title: Image, container, volume
rows: What files and defaults have we packaged?
What running instance did we create?
bottom: Finish with docker compose down — keep the counter; free the port.
notes: Have pairs show their own root Dockerfile, .dockerignore and compose.yaml before explaining the concepts. Answer: image = packaged files/default startup metadata; container = runnable instance with writable layer/runtime config; volume = storage independent of container removal. Ask which kernel is used on Mac (Linux in Desktop environment/VM). Ask whether redis:6379 is an image tag (no: host and port). down stops/removes containers/network while preserving our named volume. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-an-image/ ; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/down/
